video_title: Lawfare Daily: Aya Ibrahim on Progressive Priorities for the New Democratic Congress
gist: Former Biden NEC/OSTP official Aya Ibrahim (AI Now Institute) and host Peter Herrell discuss the agenda for the newly elected Democratic Congress: using funding fights over the Iran war, clawing back post-9/11 and emergency (IEEPA, DPA) powers, and questioning national-security framing of China policy, data centers and the AI race. Ibrahim pushes AI liability, regulatory parity for AI entrants in regulated sectors, antitrust skepticism of 'national champions', and a 'peacetime economy' focus over Pentagon-centered spending.

themes.theme: Post-election Democratic Congress: mandate and tactics

insights.claim: Aya Ibrahim frames the November election, in which Democrats won House and Senate majorities, as driven by cost of living and corruption, with the Iran war and AI/data-center fights fitting both buckets.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Expect the new Congress to prioritize affordability and anti-corruption messaging; sectors seen as symbols of corruption or cost pressure face headline risk.
insights.quote: this uh election was largely about cost of living and corruption and you can put everything sort of in those two buckets

insights.claim: Ibrahim argues the new Democratic Congress should use every tool, including bills the president will veto, investigations and subpoenas, to show voters where obstacles lie, citing Bush's jump from one veto before 2006 to 11 afterward.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Anticipate a high volume of messaging bills, subpoenas and oversight investigations in 2027-28 that create headline risk for administration-linked companies, even if few become law.
insights.quote: bills, uh, investigations, subpoenas, everything like every tool at our disposal we should be using

insights.claim: Ibrahim sees housing, and possibly the bipartisan permitting reform bill already advancing, as the most plausible areas where a progressive Congress could reach deals with President Trump.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Housing and permitting reform are the likeliest areas for actual legislation under divided government; watch homebuilders, construction and energy-infrastructure permitting.

insights.claim: Both speakers expect the next continuing resolution (CR) and Iran war funding to be the first real test of Democratic opposition, with real constraint coming only through funding restrictions rather than non-binding resolutions, and intra-party splits likely.
insights.speaker: Peter Herrell
insights.so_what: Watch the lame-duck CR and early-2027 appropriations for defense-funding restrictions; it is a near-term catalyst for defense contractors and government-shutdown risk.
insights.quote: where rubber meets the road is are Democrats going to put you know funding restrictions or uh you know reduce funding in ways that might actually constrain the war

insights.claim: Ibrahim says part of the mandate is to roll back post-9/11 national security authorities and reduce the reach of the national security state and defense spending, which she says voters do not accept and which has not worked.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: A progressive bloc pushing to cut defense spending and executive authorities is a longer-term headwind for defense budgets and Pentagon-dependent contractors.

insights.claim: Ibrahim predicts the defense budget and Pentagon spending will be front and center over the next two years and in 2028, because nearly all discretionary spending sits in the Pentagon while voters are demanding affordability.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Defense primes face rising political risk to topline budgets; watch the 2028 platform debates on Pentagon spending.
insights.quote: all of our discretionary spending is in the Pentagon

themes.theme: Executive emergency powers: IEEPA, tariffs and clawback

insights.claim: Peter Herrell notes the Supreme Court ruled Trump's IEEPA-based tariffs unlawful, and says he has pushed for a decade for reforms letting Congress claw back IEEPA power, but meets resistance from moderate and progressive Democrats who want to use it themselves.
insights.speaker: Peter Herrell
insights.so_what: Durable IEEPA reform is uncertain because both parties like the tool; tariff and sanctions policy risk via executive action stays structurally high.

insights.claim: Herrell observes that some progressive trade-policy advocates now favor expansive interpretations of tariff powers to pursue pro-labor goals, setting up an intra-Democratic debate over whether to strip executive trade powers or keep them for a future Democratic president.
insights.speaker: Peter Herrell
insights.so_what: Even under a future Democratic president, aggressive tariff use for labor goals is plausible, so do not assume tariff risk falls with a change of party.

insights.claim: Ibrahim argues trade and tech policy are being used as substitutes for broader economic policy (trade is not a substitute for raising the minimum wage) and as vehicles for factions to push existing priors, often with national security exceptionalism used to avoid democratic debate.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Expect trade and tech measures to keep carrying non-trade objectives, which makes them harder to predict from economics alone.
insights.quote: Trade is not a substitute for us raising the minimum wage, for example.

themes.theme: US-China strategy: managed trade vs. hawkish revival

insights.claim: Herrell describes Trump's second-term China policy as having moved, after the April trade war backfired when China cut off rare earths, toward a 'strategic stability' or managed-trade approach with regular summits with Xi Jinping.
insights.speaker: Peter Herrell
insights.so_what: China's rare-earth leverage disciplined US escalation; managed trade and summit cadence mean lower odds of sudden full decoupling, but rare-earth supply stays a key pressure point.
insights.quote: he certainly had his trade war back in April that kind of blew up in his face uh back in April of last year that kind of blew up in his face when China cut off rare earth

insights.claim: Herrell sees a split in the Democratic Party between national security hawks who see a political opening to out-hawk Trump on China and progressives who favor détente with selected areas of cooperation.
insights.speaker: Peter Herrell
insights.so_what: Democratic China policy is not set; a hawkish turn would raise export-control and tariff risk for China-exposed companies, a détente turn would lower it.

insights.claim: Herrell argues the Biden administration got wrong its early neglect of dialogue with China and its failure to state a stable end-state, which made Beijing disbelieve the 'small yard, high fence' export-control framing.
insights.speaker: Peter Herrell
insights.so_what: Without a stated end-state, export controls tend to widen; semiconductor firms should expect controls to grow unless policy explicitly says where they stop.

insights.claim: Both speakers say the 'small yard, high fence' export-control perimeter kept expanding in practice, illustrated by a European meme showing a chateau with vast grounds captioned as Jake Sullivan's yard.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Allies and China read US tech controls as steadily expanding; price in continued scope creep of chip and tech export controls.
insights.quote: the yard was bigger than we said it was

insights.claim: Ibrahim says restrictions on Chinese connected vehicles were really about protecting the US auto industry but were sold as 'spy car' security risks, while US tech companies, Teslas included, collect similar data without guardrails.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Security-framed trade barriers on Chinese EVs are really industrial policy and likely to persist; a privacy push could also hit US automakers' and platforms' connected-car data practices.

insights.claim: Ibrahim argues inequality harms most Americans more than China does, and that a hollowed-out government only acts in crises and so invents foreign foils instead of pursuing domestic prosperity.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Progressive policymakers may favor domestic redistribution over China-hawk industrial policy, shifting where government money goes.
insights.quote: China's not the reason they can't afford rent

themes.theme: Corporate concentration, cyber vulnerability and national champions

insights.claim: Herrell notes that despite largely removing Huawei and ZTE equipment from major US carriers (with rip-and-replace funding for small rural carriers), Chinese hackers revealed in 2024-2025 reportedly got into US telecom networks, including FBI lawful-intercept infrastructure, through older US-made routers.
insights.speaker: Peter Herrell
insights.so_what: Supply-chain bans do not secure networks; expect pressure for mandatory security standards on incumbent US network-equipment vendors and carriers, which supports cybersecurity spending.

insights.claim: Ibrahim argues it is more outrageous that US networks are so easily hacked than that competitors hack them, and that dominant vendors such as Cisco and Oracle face no forced baseline security requirements because they are too big and entrenched.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk for entrenched infrastructure vendors: a Democratic Congress could push liability or baseline cybersecurity mandates.
insights.quote: It is more outrageous that our networks that our systems are so easily hacked than it is a competitor would be hacking it

insights.claim: Ibrahim argues US big tech firms are privately held equivalents of China's state-backed national champions, the same concentration of power, and that the US keeps confusing American companies' interests with the national interest.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Progressive skepticism of the 'national champion' argument signals continued antitrust and regulatory pressure on megacap tech even if national-security arguments are made for them.
insights.quote: But we have an equivalent. They're just privately held.

insights.claim: Herrell frames a split between large US companies and hyperscalers, who say they need scale and light-touch regulation to beat China in markets like Brazil, and Tim Woo's view that US tech leadership comes from competition and upstarts, such as after the AT&T breakup.
insights.speaker: Peter Herrell
insights.so_what: The competitive-dynamism argument gives antitrust enforcers a national-security rationale, which undercuts hyperscalers' scale defense against breakups or merger limits.

insights.claim: The speakers float the counterfactual that Facebook's dominance, built by acquiring Instagram and WhatsApp during the Obama administration, pushed social-media innovation abroad, so a TikTok-like product came from China rather than the US.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Supports retroactive scrutiny of big-tech acquisitions and M&A risk for dominant platforms buying would-be rivals.

insights.claim: Ibrahim says the CHIPS and Science Act was authorized with bipartisan support, but only the CHIPS corporate subsidies were funded, while the science, university and workforce parts went largely unfunded.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Semiconductor manufacturing subsidies got funded while the research pipeline did not; watch whether a Democratic Congress funds the science part, which matters for universities and R&D-linked firms.
insights.quote: we only funded CHIPS. We made sure that we had money for the subsidies and the rest of it kind of went to the wayside

insights.claim: Both speakers ridicule chipmakers' claimed ignorance of AI chip diversion such as 'chip leakage in Singapore', arguing that sellers of server racks priced at millions of dollars each can track where their products end up.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Expect a push for tougher end-use checks and liability for AI-chip vendors on diversion via Singapore and other transshipment hubs, a compliance and revenue risk for GPU sellers.
insights.quote: how did we get this chip leakage in Singapore? I don't know. I feel like these giant companies have a good sense of where stuff's going.

themes.theme: Data centers, AI politics and national-security litigation

insights.claim: Ibrahim says opposition to data centers is an 80-20 issue with voters, with heavy bipartisan organizing, and that AI is a proxy fight over who controls the economy and democracy.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Local opposition to data centers is lopsided and bipartisan; expect more siting delays, permitting fights and costs for hyperscaler and AI-infrastructure buildouts.
insights.quote: data centers are an 8020 issue. So that that ship has sort of sailed.

insights.claim: The Trump administration has filed in an NAACP lawsuit against an xAI data center near Nashville, Tennessee, powered by gas turbines over community opposition, asking for dismissal on national security grounds because Grok is used at DoD.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Federal intervention backs AI data centers against local suits; how the case comes out sets a precedent for whether national-security claims can override environmental and civil-rights litigation against AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: we now have Grock all up in DoD. And so we need it for stuff.

insights.claim: Ibrahim says she believes, though unconfirmed, that the administration may have made a similar national-security argument in the New York Times copyright case over AI model training.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: If national-security defenses get traction in AI copyright suits, it would lower legal liability for AI labs; watch court filings.

insights.claim: Herrell, who filed an amicus brief, explains the Trump administration used the Defense Production Act to require an oil company to restart California offshore production, in effect overriding local environmental permits, and warns a favorable ruling could be used to override local opposition to data centers.
insights.speaker: Peter Herrell
insights.so_what: Watch the California DPA litigation: a favorable precedent could become a federal tool to force through data-center and energy projects, de-risking AI infrastructure siting.
insights.quote: if they get favorable court president in this oil production context, could then try to use the DPA

insights.claim: Ibrahim warns that a narrative calling data-center organizing Chinese interference could justify foreign-interference tools against Americans organizing locally.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Escalating national-security framing of data-center opposition signals political pressure to fast-track AI infrastructure, while raising backlash risk.

insights.claim: Ibrahim says AI tech leaders' public statements, such as dismissing water-usage concerns, come across as cartoonishly villainous and feed voter backlash, alongside anger at Congress for doing nothing on platform and child-safety regulation.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Reputational backlash raises the odds of child-safety and chatbot regulation; consumer AI and social platforms face policy risk.

themes.theme: AI regulatory agenda: liability, sector parity, labor safety net

insights.claim: Ibrahim proposes clear liability for AI developers whose agents commit crimes or cause harm, calling the current ambiguity an obvious gap.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Agentic-AI liability legislation is a likely Democratic priority; it would raise compliance and insurance costs for AI labs deploying agents.
insights.quote: if you are putting out agents into the world and they're committing crimes or they're causing harm, like you should be on the hook

insights.claim: Ibrahim argues AI entrants into regulated sectors such as banking and healthcare should face the same requirements as incumbents, rather than effectively deregulating those sectors by entering them.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Regulatory parity would remove AI-native fintech and healthtech companies' regulatory-arbitrage edge and protect incumbents' compliance moats.

insights.claim: Ibrahim dismisses superintelligence as an organizing focus because it is unscientific and cannot be falsified, and prefers concrete harms and liability.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Progressive AI policy is likely to target concrete harms (liability, discrimination, labor) rather than frontier-model existential-risk licensing.

insights.claim: Ibrahim says AI job displacement of white-collar workers will collide with employer-tied health insurance, Medicaid cuts, cut ACA subsidies and double-digit premium increases, creating a coalition for structural safety-net reform like the pandemic response.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: AI-driven layoffs could spur health-insurance and UI reform; watch the exposure of managed-care and insurers to policy shifts.
insights.quote: you weren't going to have investment bankers or coders making six figures who were potentially going to see themselves without a job

insights.claim: Ibrahim describes the Biden-era Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights as five design-stage principles for AI and automated systems (safe and effective, protection from algorithmic discrimination, data privacy, notice and explanation, human fallback), and says it got stuck in national-security interagency pushback.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
entities: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights
insights.so_what: These principles are a likely template for Democratic AI legislation; firms deploying automated decision systems (credit, mortgages, hiring) should expect notice, explanation and human-fallback requirements.

insights.claim: Ibrahim rejects the 'AI race with China' argument as undefined, asking how big a lead is enough and what it buys, and says the economy feels leveraged to the hilt to finance the AI buildout, with gains going mainly to people who get rich when AI IPOs hit.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: A skeptical Democratic Congress may challenge the race framing behind AI subsidies and permissive policy; there is also political risk around the leverage financing the AI capex boom.
insights.quote: Our entire economy feels leveraged to the hilt to finance this buildout.

insights.claim: Ibrahim cites a figure that over half of Americans worry someone in their household will lose their job to AI.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Widespread anxiety about AI job losses creates political demand for worker protections and backlash against AI deployment.

themes.theme: Peacetime economy vs. national-security economic policy

insights.claim: Both speakers invoke Coretta Scott King's 1970s testimony that the US has never honestly dealt with a peacetime economy, arguing economic policy is increasingly run through the national-security state, for example border measures justified by China.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Expect a progressive push to separate industrial and trade policy from national-security framing, which could weaken security-based justifications for tariffs and subsidies.
insights.quote: We've never honestly dealt with the question of a peace time economy.

insights.claim: Ibrahim argues that if everything is treated as an emergency or a national-security matter, nothing really is, and that national-security exceptionalism is eroding both governance and citizens' ability to sue and push back.
insights.speaker: Aya Ibrahim
insights.so_what: Courts and Congress may push back on emergency and national-security justifications (IEEPA, DPA), creating legal risk for policies and projects that depend on them.
